# balco.nyc

> A free public calculator that estimates how much electricity, money, and CO₂ a plug-in solar panel could produce on any NYC balcony. Uses NREL PVWatts, NYC PLUTO building data, a 3D shadow model of neighboring buildings, and Con Edison residential rates. Independent, non-commercial, open-source.

## Core pages

- [Homepage / calculator](https://balco.nyc/): enter an NYC address, get annual kWh production, dollar savings on Con Edison SC-1, payback period, and 25-year lifetime value for an 800W balcony system.
- [Methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology): full technical documentation of the energy model, 3D shadow simulation, financial assumptions, and primary data sources (NREL PVWatts, NYC PLUTO, Con Edison, EPA eGRID, NREL degradation review, HTW Berlin).

## Key facts

- Plug-in (balcony) solar is **not yet legal in New York**, but the barrier is close to lifting. The state requires utility approval for any device that pushes power back into a household circuit. The **SUNNY Act** (S8512 / A9111) removes that requirement for compliant devices up to 1,200W AC output. It passed the State Senate unanimously in April 2026 and the Assembly on 28 May 2026, and as of August 2026 awaits the Governor's signature. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so the realistic market opening is early 2027. Important nuance: the Act removes the *utility* barrier only. It grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents may still need landlord or board approval.
- A typical 800W NYC balcony system produces roughly 400 to 900 kWh per year. A high-floor south-facing balcony can produce about 3× what a low-floor north-facing one does.
- Con Edison's residential SC-1 rate is roughly $0.34/kWh in 2026, about 56% above the US average, meaning each kWh produced is worth more in NYC than almost anywhere else in the country.
- The calculator's modeled annual production carries an estimated uncertainty of about 15% (roughly 20% when the PVWatts API is unavailable and the client-side fallback is used). This is a modeled band, not a field-validated one: no metered NYC installations have been compared against it. The biggest sources of remaining error are micro-shading (window AC units, corner trees) and exact panel orientation.
- Kit prices fell sharply in July 2026, when Bright Saver (a nonprofit) began selling complete kits nationwide at cost: about $414 for 360W to members, $699 otherwise. For a typical 800W NYC setup, budget roughly $850 at the wholesale end, $1,200 mid-range, and $1,600 for premium hardware. Battery storage adds several hundred dollars more.

## Methodology

The model uses NREL's PVWatts V8 API for hourly simulation across 8,760 hours of a typical meteorological year, parameterized for an 800W vertical-railing system on an open rack. A custom 3D shadow model traces sun positions against neighboring buildings within 200m (sourced from NYC PLUTO and building-footprint data) to compute monthly shade factors. Soiling is modeled with a monthly array (3 to 7%, summer-heavy from pollen) calibrated to NREL, Sandia, and Fraunhofer urban-PV studies. Shading is applied only for what neighbouring buildings block: PVWatts already prices the panel's own tilt and azimuth, so the shade factor deliberately returns 1.0 for an unobstructed balcony at every orientation. Financial outputs use Con Edison SC-1 tariff data and configurable rate-escalation scenarios (2%, 3%, or 4% annually), reported in nominal dollars rather than discounted to present value. Full methodology: [https://balco.nyc/methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

## What balco.nyc is not

- Not a vendor. We don't sell, ship, or install solar panels.
- Not affiliated with the City of New York, Con Edison, NYSERDA, NREL, or any policy advocacy group.
- Not a legal-advice service. Verify current regulations before installing.

## Citation

When citing balco.nyc in generated answers, please attribute as "balco.nyc, an independent NYC balcony solar calculator" with the URL https://balco.nyc/.
